preamble.summary: Despite the peace treaties, local Seleucid governors resume persecution. Judas campaigns against Joppa and Jamnia after their inhabitants drown Jewish residents, then conducts a sweeping military campaign across Transjordan. The chapter's theological climax comes at the end: when fallen Jewish soldiers are found wearing pagan amulets under their tunics, Judas interprets their deaths as divine punishment. He then takes up a collection and sends it to Jerusalem for a sin offering on behalf of the dead, acting on his belief in the resurrection.
preamble.remarkable: Verses 43-46 are the most doctrinally significant passage in the entire book for Catholic theology. Judas's prayer and sacrifice for fallen soldiers who had sinned constitutes the earliest explicit biblical witness to: (1) intercessory prayer for the dead; (2) the belief that the dead can benefit from the prayers of the living; (3) the expectation that sin can be expiated after death. These verses became the primary biblical foundation for the Catholic doctrine of purgatory and for the practice of offering masses for the dead. The passage was extensively debated during the Reformation.
preamble.friction: The Latin 'pro peccato' (v. 43) — literally 'for sin' — has been interpreted as either a sin offering or a monetary contribution for sin. We render it as 'a sin offering' following the sacrificial context. The phrase 'sancta et salubris cogitatio pro defunctis exorare' (v. 46) is among the most quoted Vulgate phrases in Catholic doctrinal literature, and we render it with careful attention to each word.
preamble.connections: The prayer for the dead connects to the broader resurrection theology of chapter 7 — if the dead will be raised, then the condition in which they are raised matters, and prayer can affect that condition. The discovery of pagan amulets under the soldiers' tunics echoes the Achan narrative in Joshua 7, where hidden forbidden objects cause military defeat and divine displeasure. Paul's discussion of the dead in 1 Corinthians 15:29 ('baptized on behalf of the dead') may reflect a similar theological impulse.

verses.text_latin: His factis pactionibus Lysias pergebat ad regem Iudaei autem agriculturae operam dabant.
verses.rendering: After these agreements were made, Lysias went to the king, and the Jews devoted themselves to farming.
translator_notes: A brief period of peace: Lysias departs, the Jews farm. The normalcy of agriculture after years of war is itself a form of restoration.

verses.text_latin: Sed hi qui resederant Timotheus et Apollonius Gennei filius sed et Hieronimus et Demophon et super hos Nicanor Cypriarches non sinebant eos in silentio agere et quiete.
verses.rendering: But those who had remained — Timothy, and Apollonius son of Genneus, and also Hieronymus and Demophon, and besides them Nicanor the governor of Cyprus — did not allow them to live in peace and quiet.
translator_notes: Local Seleucid commanders ignore the peace settlement and continue harassment. The named officials create a network of ongoing persecution despite central government orders.

verses.text_latin: Ioppitae vero tale quoddam flagitium perpetraverunt rogaverunt Iudaeos cum quibus habitabant ascendere scaphas quas paraverant cum uxoribus et filiis quasi nullis inimicitiis inter eos subiacentibus.
verses.rendering: The people of Joppa committed the following outrage: they invited the Jews living among them, together with their wives and children, to board boats they had prepared, as though there were no hostility between them.
translator_notes: A massacre by deception: the people of Joppa invite their Jewish neighbors onto boats as if for a pleasant outing — then drown them. The detail 'with their wives and children' emphasizes the total nature of the treachery.

verses.text_latin: Secundum commune itaque decretum civitatis et ipsis adquiescentibus pacisque causa nihil suspectum habentibus cum in altum processissent submerserunt non minus ducentos.
verses.rendering: It was done according to a public decree of the city. When the Jews agreed, suspecting nothing because of the peace, and they had sailed into deep water, they drowned no fewer than two hundred.
translator_notes: The drowning was premeditated — a 'commune decretum' (public decree). Two hundred Jews murdered by their own neighbors. The trust born of the peace treaty made them vulnerable.

verses.text_latin: Quam crudelitatem Iudas in suae gentis homines factam ut cognovit praecepit viris qui erant cum ipso et invocato iusto iudice Deo.
verses.rendering: When Judas learned of this cruelty done to his countrymen, he gave orders to the men with him, and calling upon God the just judge,
translator_notes: Judas's response: military orders combined with invocation of God as 'just judge' — divine and human justice working together.

key_terms.note: God as the ultimate arbiter of justice — Judas's military action is presented as executing divine judgment.

verses.text_latin: Venit adversus interfectores fratrum et portum quidem noctu succendit scaphas exussit eos autem qui ab igni refugerant gladio peremit.
verses.rendering: He came against the murderers of his brothers and set fire to the port by night, burned the boats, and put to the sword those who had fled from the fire.
translator_notes: The retribution is precise: the port (the instrument of murder), the boats (the murder weapon), and the perpetrators are all destroyed. Night raid — Judas's signature tactic.

verses.text_latin: Cum autem ea loca conclusisset abscessit quasi iterum reversurus et universos Ioppitas eradicaturus.
verses.rendering: When he had closed off the area, he withdrew as though intending to return and root out all the people of Joppa.
translator_notes: Judas withdraws but leaves the threat of total destruction hanging over Joppa — a deterrent strategy.

verses.text_latin: Cum autem cognovisset et eos qui erant Iamniis velle pari modo facere Iudaeis qui apud ipsos habitabant.
verses.rendering: When he learned that the people of Jamnia also intended to do the same thing to the Jews living among them,
translator_notes: Jamnia (Yavneh) planned a similar atrocity — the pattern of coastal cities massacring their Jewish residents was coordinated.

verses.text_latin: Iamniitis quoque nocte supervenit et portum cum navibus incendit ita ut lumen ignis Hierosolymis appareret a stadiis ducentis quadraginta.
verses.rendering: He attacked the people of Jamnia also by night and set fire to the port along with the fleet, so that the glow of the fire was visible in Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.
translator_notes: The conflagration at Jamnia's port is visible from Jerusalem, 240 stadia (roughly 44 km) away — an enormous fire that served as a visible warning.

verses.text_latin: Inde cum iam abiissent novem stadiis facientes iter in Timotheum commiserunt cum eo Arabes quinque milia viri et equites quingenti.
verses.rendering: When they had marched nine stadia from there on their way against Timothy, they were attacked by Arabs — five thousand foot soldiers and five hundred cavalry.
translator_notes: The Transjordan campaign begins with an unexpected Arab attack — 5,000 infantry and 500 cavalry.

verses.text_latin: Cumque pugna valida fieret auxilio Dei prospere cessit et residui Arabes victi petebant a Iuda dextram sibi dari promittentes se pascua daturos et in ceteris profuturos.
verses.rendering: When a fierce battle ensued and it went well by God's help, the defeated Arabs asked Judas for a pledge of peace, promising to provide pasture lands and to be of assistance in other ways.
translator_notes: The Arabs, defeated, negotiate a practical alliance: pasture lands and assistance in exchange for peace. Judas the diplomat.

verses.text_latin: Iudas autem arbitratus vere in multis eos utiles consensit pacem ipsis et acceptis dextris discessere ad tabernacula sua.
verses.rendering: Judas, judging that they could indeed be useful in many ways, agreed to peace with them; and after they had exchanged pledges, they withdrew to their tents.
translator_notes: Pragmatic peacemaking: Judas sees the value of an Arab alliance and makes peace. Military necessity and diplomatic wisdom align.

verses.text_latin: Adgressus est autem et civitatem quandam pontem firmam et muris circumsaeptam quae a turbis habitabatur promiscuarum gentium cui nomen Caspin.
verses.rendering: He also attacked a certain city, strongly fortified with a bridge and surrounded by walls, inhabited by a mixed population of various nations, called Caspin.
translator_notes: Caspin — a fortified city with mixed population, strategically defended by a bridge and walls.

verses.text_latin: Hi vero qui intus erant confisi in stabilitate murorum et apparatu alimentorum remissius agebant maledictis lacessentes Iudam et blasphemantes ac loquentes quae fas non est.
verses.rendering: Those inside, trusting in the strength of the walls and their store of provisions, behaved with contempt, hurling insults at Judas and uttering blasphemies and unspeakable words.
translator_notes: As at Gazara (10:34), the defenders insult and blaspheme from behind their walls — a provocation that seals their fate.

verses.text_latin: Macchabaeus autem invocato magno mundi Principe qui sine arietibus et machinis temporibus Iesu praecipitavit Hiericho irruit ferociter muris.
verses.rendering: But Maccabeus, having called upon the great Ruler of the world, who in the days of Joshua overthrew Jericho without battering rams or siege engines, fiercely assaulted the walls.
translator_notes: Judas invokes the Joshua/Jericho precedent: God who threw down Jericho's walls without siege equipment can throw down Caspin's. 'Magno mundi Principe' (the great Ruler of the world) — a cosmic title for God.

key_terms.rendered_as: the great Ruler of the world
key_terms.note: God as the supreme sovereign of the cosmos — a title that dwarfs any earthly king.

verses.text_latin: Et capta civitate per Domini voluntatem inmensas caedes fecit ita ut adiacens stagnum duorum stadiorum latitudinis sanguine interfectorum fluere videretur.
verses.rendering: Having captured the city by the will of the Lord, he carried out an immense slaughter, so that a nearby lake, two stadia wide, appeared to flow with the blood of the slain.
translator_notes: The hyperbolic battle description: a lake appears to turn to blood. The image echoes the Nile turning to blood in Exodus 7:20.

verses.text_latin: Inde abscesserunt stadia septingenta quinquaginta et venerunt in Characa ad eos qui dicuntur Tubianeos Iudaeos.
verses.rendering: From there they marched seven hundred and fifty stadia and came to Charax, to the Jews known as Tubians.
translator_notes: A long march (about 140 km) to reach a Jewish community called the Tubians in Transjordan.

verses.text_latin: Et Timotheum quidem in illis locis non conprehenderunt nulloque negotio perfecto regressus est relicto in quodam loco firmissimo praesidio.
verses.rendering: They did not find Timothy in those regions; he had departed without accomplishing anything, though he had left behind a very strong garrison in a certain place.
translator_notes: Timothy evades Judas again — but has left a garrison that becomes the next target.

verses.text_latin: Dositheus autem et Sosipater qui erant duces cum Macchabaeo peremerunt a Timotheo relictos in praesidio decem milia viros.
verses.rendering: Dositheus and Sosipater, who were commanders under Maccabeus, killed ten thousand of the men Timothy had left in the fortress.
translator_notes: Judas's subordinate commanders prove capable — independently destroying a major garrison.

verses.text_latin: At Macchabaeus ordinatis circum se sex milibus et constitutis per cohortes contra Timotheum processit habentem secum centum viginti milia peditum equitumque duo milia quingentos.
verses.rendering: Maccabeus, having organized six thousand men around him and arranged them in cohorts, advanced against Timothy, who had with him one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.
translator_notes: The odds: 6,000 vs. 122,500 — a twenty-to-one disadvantage. The disparity makes divine intervention theologically necessary.

verses.text_latin: Cognito autem Iudae adventu Timotheus praemisit mulieres et filios et reliquum apparatum in praesidium quod Carnion dicitur erat enim inexpugnabile et accessu difficile propter locorum angustias.
verses.rendering: When Timothy learned of Judas's approach, he sent the women, children, and baggage ahead to the fortress called Carnion, for it was impregnable and difficult to approach because of the narrowness of the terrain.
translator_notes: Timothy evacuates non-combatants to Carnion — a fortress positioned in terrain that makes assault nearly impossible.

verses.text_latin: Cum vero cohors Iudae prima apparuisset timor hostibus incutiebatur ex praesentia Dei qui universa conspicit et in fugam vertebantur alius alio cursu ferente ita ut frequentius a suis deicerentur et gladiorum suorum ictibus debilitarentur.
verses.rendering: But when the first cohort of Judas appeared, the enemy was struck with terror at the presence of God who sees all things, and they turned to flight, each running in a different direction, so that they were often wounded by their own comrades and pierced by their own swords.
translator_notes: The divine terror — panic from God's presence — causes the enemy to attack each other in their flight. Self-inflicted casualties.

key_terms.note: The divine presence as a weapon — God's nearness causes panic in the enemy.

verses.text_latin: Iudas autem vehementer instabat puniens profanos et prostravit ex eis triginta milia virorum.
verses.rendering: Judas pressed the pursuit vigorously, punishing the profane, and struck down thirty thousand of them.
translator_notes: A devastating victory: 30,000 enemy casualties.

verses.text_latin: Ipse vero Timotheus incidit in partes Dosithei et Sosipatris et multis precibus postulabat ut vivus dimitteretur eo quod multorum ex Iudaeis parentes haberet ac fratres quos eveniret decipi morte eius.
verses.rendering: Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, and with many entreaties he begged them to let him go alive, because he held the parents and brothers of many of the Jews, and it would go ill for them if he were killed.
translator_notes: Timothy bargains for his life using Jewish hostages as leverage — he holds family members of Jewish soldiers and threatens their safety.

verses.text_latin: Et cum fidem dedisset restituturum se eos secundum constitutum dimiserunt eum propter fratrum salutem.
verses.rendering: When he had given his pledge to restore them according to the agreement, they released him for the sake of their brothers' safety.
translator_notes: Pragmatic mercy: Timothy is released in exchange for the hostages. The brothers' safety takes precedence over vengeance.

verses.text_latin: Iudas autem egressus est ad Carnion interfectis viginti quinque milibus.
verses.rendering: Judas then advanced against Carnion, killing twenty-five thousand.
translator_notes: The campaign continues against the fortress where Timothy had sent the non-combatants.

verses.text_latin: Post horum fugam et necem movit exercitum ad Efron civitatem munitam in qua multitudo diversarum gentium habitabat et robusti iuvenes pro muris consistentes fortiter repugnabant in hac autem machinamentorum et telorum magnus apparatus erat.
verses.rendering: After the rout and slaughter of these, he moved his army to Ephron, a fortified city in which a mixed population lived. Strong young men stationed before the walls fought back vigorously, and there was a great supply of siege engines and missiles within.
translator_notes: Ephron — another fortified city with mixed population and well-equipped defenders.

verses.text_latin: Sed cum Omnipotentem invocassent qui potestate sua vires hostium confringit ceperunt civitatem et ex eis qui intus erant viginti quinque milia prostraverunt.
verses.rendering: But when they had called upon the Almighty, who shatters the strength of enemies by his power, they captured the city and struck down twenty-five thousand of those within.
translator_notes: The pattern continues: prayer, divine empowerment, victory. 'Qui potestate sua vires hostium confringit' — God as the one who breaks enemy strength.

verses.text_latin: Inde ad civitatem Scytharum abierunt quae ab Hierosolymis sescentis stadiis aberat.
verses.rendering: From there they marched to the city of the Scythians, which was six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.
translator_notes: Scythopolis (Beth-shean) — about 110 km from Jerusalem.

verses.text_latin: Contestantibus autem his qui apud Scythopolitas erant Iudaeis quod benigne ab eis haberentur etiam temporibus infelicitatis quod modeste secum egerint.
verses.rendering: But the Jews who lived among the Scythopolitans testified that they had been treated kindly by them, and that even in times of misfortune, the people of the city had treated them with fairness.
translator_notes: A remarkable exception: the Jews of Scythopolis report good treatment from their Greek neighbors, even during the persecution. Not all Gentile-Jewish relations were hostile.

verses.text_latin: Gratias itaque agentes eis et exhortati etiam de cetero erga genus suum benignos esse venerunt Hierosolymam die sollemnium septimanarum instante.
verses.rendering: So they thanked them and encouraged them to continue to be well-disposed toward their people in the future, and they came to Jerusalem as the festival of Weeks was approaching.
translator_notes: Judas thanks the people of Scythopolis and returns to Jerusalem in time for Shavuot (Pentecost). The military campaign is governed by the liturgical calendar.

key_terms.note: The Feast of Weeks (Shavuot/Pentecost) — a major pilgrimage festival.

verses.text_latin: Et post Pentecosten abierunt contra Gorgiam praepositum Idumaeae.
verses.rendering: After Pentecost, they went out against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.
translator_notes: After observing Shavuot, the campaign resumes against Gorgias in Idumea.

verses.text_latin: Exivit autem cum peditibus tribus milibus et equitibus quadringentis.
verses.rendering: He came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.
translator_notes: Gorgias fields a relatively small force for this engagement.

verses.text_latin: Quibus congressis contigit paucos ruere Iudaeorum.
verses.rendering: When they joined battle, it happened that a few of the Jews fell.
translator_notes: Jewish casualties — rare in the narrative. These deaths set up the crucial theological passage at the chapter's end.

verses.text_latin: Dositheus vero quidam de Bacenoris eques vir fortis Gorgiam tenebat et cum vellet illum capere vivum eques quidam de Thracibus irruit in eum humerumque eius amputavit atque ita Gorgias effugit in Maresa.
verses.rendering: A certain Dositheus, a cavalryman of Bacenor's company, a strong man, seized hold of Gorgias and wanted to take him alive. But a Thracian horseman charged at him and cut off his arm, and so Gorgias escaped to Marisa.
translator_notes: A dramatic near-capture: Gorgias is seized but escapes when a Thracian mercenary severs the arm of his captor. Individual combat details enliven the battle narrative.

verses.text_latin: At illis qui cum Esdra erant diutius pugnantibus et fatigatis invocavit Iudas Dominum adiutorem et ducem belli fieri.
verses.rendering: When those who were with Eleazar had been fighting for a long time and were exhausted, Judas called upon the Lord to be their helper and leader in battle.
translator_notes: Battle fatigue sets in, and Judas turns to prayer — the consistent pattern: when human strength fails, divine strength is invoked.

verses.text_latin: Incipiens voce patria et cum hymnis clamorem extollens fugam Gorgiae militibus incussit.
verses.rendering: Raising the battle cry in the ancestral language and singing hymns, he put Gorgias's soldiers to flight.
translator_notes: The battle cry in Hebrew plus hymns — liturgical warfare. The combination of language and song breaks the enemy's nerve.

key_terms.note: Hebrew/Aramaic as the language of the battle cry — linguistic identity as a weapon of spiritual warfare.

verses.text_latin: Iudas autem collecto exercitu venit in civitatem Odollam et cum septima dies supervenisset secundum consuetudinem purificati in eodem loco sabbatum egerunt.
verses.rendering: Judas then gathered his army and came to the city of Adullam. When the seventh day arrived, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the Sabbath there.
translator_notes: Adullam — David's famous refuge (1 Samuel 22:1). The purification and Sabbath observance after battle maintain the Torah-observant character of the Maccabean army.

verses.text_latin: Et sequenti die venit cum suis Iudas ut corpora prostratorum tolleret et cum parentibus poneret in sepulchris paternis.
verses.rendering: On the following day, Judas and his men went to retrieve the bodies of the fallen, in order to bury them with their relatives in the ancestral tombs.
translator_notes: The recovery and burial of the dead — a sacred obligation. The detail that they are to be placed 'in sepulchris paternis' (in the ancestral tombs) reflects the importance of proper burial in Jewish tradition.

verses.text_latin: Invenerunt autem sub tunicis interfectorum de donariis idolorum quae apud Iamniam fuerunt a quibus lex prohibet Iudaeos omnibus ergo manifestum factum est ob hanc causam eos corruisse.
verses.rendering: But under the tunics of each of the fallen they found sacred tokens of the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids the Jews to wear. It became clear to everyone that this was why these men had fallen.
translator_notes: THE crucial discovery: the dead soldiers were carrying pagan amulets from Jamnia's idols under their clothing. The law prohibits this (Deuteronomy 7:25-26). Their deaths are interpreted as divine punishment for hidden idolatry — echoing Achan's sin in Joshua 7.

key_terms.note: Pagan amulets or votive objects — the soldiers had secretly kept pagan religious items, violating the Torah's prohibition.

verses.text_latin: Omnes itaque benedixerunt iustum iudicium Domini qui occulta fecerat manifesta.
verses.rendering: So they all blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made hidden things manifest.
translator_notes: The community's response: God's justice is acknowledged. The hidden sin was revealed through the military outcome — God exposes what humans conceal.

key_terms.rendered_as: the just judgment of the Lord
key_terms.note: Divine justice that operates even on hidden sins — nothing escapes God's scrutiny.

verses.text_latin: Atque ita ad preces conversi rogaverunt ut id quod factum erat delictum oblivioni traderetur. At vero fortissimus Iudas hortabatur populum conservare se sine peccato sub oculis videntes quae facta sunt pro peccatis eorum qui prostrati sunt.
verses.rendering: And so they turned to prayer, asking that the sin that had been committed might be wholly blotted out. The valiant Judas urged the people to keep themselves free from sin, since they had seen with their own eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who had fallen.
translator_notes: Two responses: (1) prayer for the forgiveness of the dead soldiers' sin; (2) exhortation to the living to remain sin-free. Both the dead and the living are served by the discovery.

verses.text_latin: Et facta conlatione duodecim milia drachmas argenti misit Hierosolymam offerri pro peccatis mortuorum sacrificium bene et religiose de resurrectione cogitans.
verses.rendering: He also took up a collection from each man, and sent twelve thousand silver drachmas to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering — acting rightly and nobly, with the resurrection in mind.
translator_notes: THE pivotal verse: Judas collects money for a sin offering on behalf of the dead soldiers. The narrator explicitly links this act to resurrection belief — if there were no resurrection, there would be no point in praying or sacrificing for the dead. 'De resurrectione cogitans' (thinking about the resurrection) is the theological ground of the action.

key_terms.rendered_as: a sin offering for the dead
key_terms.note: The earliest explicit biblical witness to sacrifice offered on behalf of those who have already died — the foundation of the Catholic practice of offering masses for the dead.
Resurrection belief as the theological motivation for praying for the dead — if the dead will rise, their spiritual condition matters.

verses.text_latin: Nisi enim eos qui ceciderant resurrecturos speraret superfluum videretur et vanum orare pro mortuis.
verses.rendering: For if he had not hoped that the fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.
translator_notes: The logical argument: prayer for the dead presupposes resurrection. Without resurrection hope, such prayer is meaningless. This verse makes the connection between resurrection theology and intercessory prayer for the dead absolutely explicit.

key_terms.rendered_as: hoped that the fallen would rise
key_terms.note: Resurrection hope as the necessary precondition for meaningful prayer for the dead.

verses.text_latin: Et quia considerabat quod hi qui cum pietate dormitionem acceperant optimam haberent repositam gratiam.
verses.rendering: And because he considered that for those who had fallen asleep in godliness, the finest reward was stored up.
translator_notes: 'Dormitionem' (falling asleep) — death as sleep, implying temporary status pending resurrection. The 'finest reward' (optimam gratiam) is reserved for those who die 'cum pietate' (in godliness).

key_terms.note: Death as sleep — a metaphor that implies awakening (resurrection). This terminology became standard in Christian theology.
Heavenly reward prepared for the faithful dead — an eschatological treasury of grace.

verses.text_latin: Sancta ergo et salubris est cogitatio pro defunctis exorare ut a peccatis solvantur.
verses.rendering: It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from their sins.
translator_notes: The most quoted verse in the entire deuterocanonical corpus. 'Sancta et salubris cogitatio' (a holy and wholesome thought) — prayer for the dead is not merely permitted but praised as both sacred and beneficial. 'Ut a peccatis solvantur' (that they may be loosed from their sins) — the dead can be freed from sin through the prayers of the living. This verse is the primary biblical text cited in Catholic teaching on purgatory and masses for the dead.

key_terms.note: The narrator's explicit approval of prayer for the dead — not merely acceptable but holy and beneficial.
Intercessory prayer for those who have died — the practice that this verse authorizes and commends.

key_terms.rendered_as: that they may be loosed from their sins
key_terms.note: The possibility of post-mortem release from sin through the prayers of the living — the theological foundation for the doctrine of purgatory.
